newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan's top envoy to visit three African allies.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan's top envoy to visit three African allies.

text.p: Taiwan's Foreign Minister John Chang began on Sunday visits to three diplomatic allies in Africa as a diplomatic tug-of-war with rival China intensified.
Chang, ending a low-key European mission, would visit Guinea-Bissau, Senegal and Sao Tome and Principe, with which it recently established ties, local newspapers reported.
The foreign minister slipped out of Taiwan on Monday for Belgium and Luxembourg in the latest of a series of secretive overseas visits to promote Taiwan's relations with Europe.
Chang played down the significance of his African visits, which start with a trip to Guinea-Bissau on Sunday.
"The allies are our friends. We have to have frequent exchanges of visits and discussions of regional issues," Chang told the United Daily News on Saturday.
"We cannot wait to make such visits until after we discover there are problems," Chang said in Luxembourg.
Taiwan newspapers said Chang added the tiny West African state of Sao Tome and Principe to his itinerary after ties, established on May 6, ran into difficulties.
Sao Tome officials said on Friday the African republic had received a pledge from Taiwan to provide aid totalling $30 million over the next decade after deciding to establish ties with Taipei.
On Saturday, Taiwan's Foreign Ministry denied reports that it had begun funding Sao Tome.
The ministry said Taiwan would offer aid to help develop Sao Tome's economy, but such aid would be provided according to a set plan and would need approval from Taiwan's parliament.
China, a diplomatic rival of Taiwan since a civil war split the two in 1949, has accused the island of trying to use money to buy international relations.

Beijing has tightened a diplomatic squeeze on Taipei in a quest to bring Taiwan under mainland rule, warning other countries not to exchange ties with Taipei or permit visits by senior Taiwan officials.
To evade China's diplomatic embargo, Taiwan has engaged in what it calls "pragmatic diplomacy" -- quiet, unofficial visits to countries that recognise Beijing instead of Taipei.
Taiwan hailed as a success Chang's address to the European Parliament in Brussels on Thursday despite strong protests from China.
Chang also met people he called several "important friends" in Luxembourg.

Since wresting the Chinese U.N. seat from Taiwan's ruling Nationalists in the 1970s, Beijing has won the recognition of most governments. Taipei now has diplomatic links with only 30 states, most of them small, poor and dependent on its financial largesse.
